specStatements.text: A system is an object or group of objects.
There are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes.
Students should be able to describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example:
• a moving object hitting an obstacle
• an object accelerated by a constant force
• bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle.
Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by:
• work done when a current flows
• use calculations to show on a common scale how the overall energy in a system is redistributed when the system is changed.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: 'For example' marks the five bulleted situations as exemplars of common situations rather than a closed list, and 'all the changes' fixes the depth of the demand. Every describing question here is set in one of the five named situations, and the correct answer always names both what empties and what fills, never only the half that is easy to see. Nothing that belongs to a later sub-section is tested: efficiency, the formal treatment of conservation and dissipation (4.1.2), power (4.1.1.5) and the national grid are all kept out, even where the context would invite them.

scopeNotes.statement: Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This statement signposts three calculation routes; the equations themselves are set out elsewhere in the Energy section. Only those equations are used here, exactly as the specification states them — ΔE = m c Δθ, W = F s and P = E / t — and each is quoted in the stem of any question that needs it. No specific heat capacity is expected from memory: every value is supplied with its unit. No equation from outside the Energy section is introduced, and no rearrangement beyond the single step the specification's own form requires is demanded.

concepts.definition: A system is an object or a group of objects. It is simply whatever you choose to treat as the thing being studied — a single stone, a stone and the Earth together, or a kettle together with the water inside it. Choosing the system first is what makes it possible to say clearly which stores are emptying and which are filling.

A way in which a system holds energy. Naming a store answers the question 'where is the energy now?' — for example the kinetic store, the gravitational potential store, the elastic potential store, the thermal store and the chemical store.
The store filled when an object moves. The faster the object moves and the greater its mass, the more energy is in its kinetic store.
The store filled when an object is raised. Its content depends on the mass of the object, its height, and the gravitational field strength.
The store filled when an object such as a spring, a rubber band or a crumpling car bumper is stretched, squashed or deformed.
The store filled when the temperature of a material rises. Almost every everyday change ends with energy in the thermal stores of the objects involved and of the surroundings.
The store held in fuels, foods and batteries, which empties when a chemical reaction such as burning or respiration takes place.
The moving of energy from one store to another. A transfer is not itself a store: the routes named in this section are heating, work done by forces and work done when a current flows.
A transfer of energy caused by a difference in temperature. Heating fills the thermal store of the cooler object and empties the store supplying the energy.
The transfer of energy that happens when a force moves an object through a distance along the line of the force. Work done is calculated using W = F s.

concepts.term: Work done when a current flows
concepts.definition: The transfer of energy that happens when charge is pushed through a component by a power supply. The energy transferred in a time t is found from P = E / t.
The spreading out of energy into thermal stores of the surroundings, where it is no longer useful. The energy is still there; it is simply shared out too thinly to be used.
A diagram in which the energy in each store, before and after a change, is drawn as a bar using the same scale throughout, so that the redistribution of a fixed total can be seen at a glance.

misconceptions.question: Does a system have to be a machine or a device?
misconceptions.correct: No. A system is simply an object or a group of objects — a stone, a beaker of water, or a car and the road it runs on.
misconceptions.misconception: A system is a machine or a piece of equipment, such as an engine or a circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'system' is used for heating systems, sound systems and computer systems, all of which are manufactured devices.
misconceptions.correction: In physics the word is deliberately far wider. The specification defines it in one line: a system is an object or group of objects. You choose the system, and nothing needs to have been built for it to count.

misconceptions.question: Can a single object be a system on its own?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The definition is 'an object or group of objects', so one object alone is a perfectly good system.
misconceptions.misconception: A system must contain at least two objects interacting with each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'group' is the part students remember, and diagrams in lessons usually show two or more objects together.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition in full. Either half satisfies it: a single falling ball is a system, and so is the ball together with the Earth. Which you choose depends on what you want to describe.

misconceptions.question: When a system changes, is energy used up?
misconceptions.correct: No. The energy is still there; what changes is the way it is stored.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is consumed, destroyed or created when something happens.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language is full of 'using energy', 'energy loss' and 'running out of energy', all of which suggest the energy has gone.
misconceptions.correction: Describe every change as stores emptying and other stores filling. 'Used up' usually means 'now in a thermal store of the surroundings, spread out too thinly to be useful'.

misconceptions.question: Is heating an energy store?
misconceptions.correct: No. Heating is a way of transferring energy between stores, not a store itself.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating, working and electricity are types of energy that a system can hold.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Older courses taught 'heat energy', 'electrical energy' and 'sound energy' as types of energy, and the habit of listing them as stores survives.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two lists apart. Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear. Transfers: heating, work done by forces, work done when a current flows, and by waves.

misconceptions.question: At the top of its flight, does a thrown ball still have energy in its kinetic store?
misconceptions.correct: If it was thrown straight up, no: at the highest point it is momentarily still, so the kinetic store is empty.
misconceptions.misconception: The ball must still hold some energy in its kinetic store, or it could not come back down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It feels as though the ball needs 'movement energy' in reserve to start moving again, and students confuse being at rest with having no energy at all.
misconceptions.correction: It comes back down because its gravitational store is now full and the weight still acts. The gravitational store empties again on the way down, refilling the kinetic store.

misconceptions.question: As an object rises, which store is filling?
misconceptions.correct: The gravitational potential store fills while the kinetic store empties.
misconceptions.misconception: The object is gaining kinetic energy because it is moving upwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Moving' is linked to 'kinetic', so any motion is taken to mean the kinetic store is filling, regardless of whether the object is speeding up or slowing down.
misconceptions.correction: The kinetic store depends on speed, not on movement as such. A ball thrown upwards slows down as it rises, so its kinetic store empties as its gravitational store fills.

misconceptions.question: A moving trolley hits a wall and stops. Is its energy destroyed?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is transferred to thermal stores of the trolley, the wall and the surroundings, and carried away by sound waves.
misconceptions.misconception: The impact destroys the energy the trolley had.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The energy becomes invisible: the trolley stops, nothing obvious moves, and a very small temperature rise cannot be felt.
misconceptions.correction: Look for where the energy has gone rather than assuming it has gone. Warm, dented metal and a loud bang are the evidence that the energy has been spread into thermal stores and waves.

misconceptions.question: Does a force store energy inside the object it pushes?
misconceptions.correct: No. A force is not a store. The work done by the force transfers energy into a store such as the kinetic store.
misconceptions.misconception: The pushing force is stored in the object and gradually gets used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force and energy are both introduced as things that make objects move, and 'the force runs out' is a natural way to explain why an object eventually stops.
misconceptions.correction: A force is an interaction, not something an object holds. When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done and energy moves between stores; the object holds energy, never force.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy go when a car brakes?
misconceptions.correct: To the thermal stores of the brakes, the tyres, the road and the air around them.
misconceptions.misconception: The kinetic store empties into the chemical store of the brakes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the brakes are where the change happens and reach for the chemical store because it is the one they associate with cars and fuel.
misconceptions.correction: Chemical stores empty in reactions such as burning; friction does not fill them. Friction between brake pad and disc does work that fills thermal stores, which is why brakes get hot.

misconceptions.question: If energy is dissipated, has the total gone down?
misconceptions.correct: No. The total is unchanged; the energy has simply been shared out into the thermal stores of the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Dissipated energy is lost, so a system ends with less energy than it started with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'lost' is used in class for wasted energy, and a warm road is much harder to picture than a moving car.
misconceptions.correction: On a common scale diagram the bars after a change always add up to the same total as before. Dissipation changes where the energy is, never how much there is.

misconceptions.question: What supplies the energy that boils water in an electric kettle?
misconceptions.correct: The mains supply. A current in the heating element does work, filling the thermal store of the element and then of the water.
misconceptions.misconception: The kettle's own chemical store empties into the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The chemical store is the one most often met as a source, and a kettle is a self-contained object that looks as though it must hold something.
misconceptions.correction: A kettle stores nothing until it is plugged in. The energy arrives from the mains while the current flows, which is why unplugging the kettle stops the heating at once.

misconceptions.question: Does a heated component hold a store of electrical energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is no electrical store. The current does work, which fills the component's thermal store.
misconceptions.misconception: The element gains electrical energy, which it holds until it is switched off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Electrical energy' was taught for years as a type of energy, and it is still used loosely in everyday writing about appliances.
misconceptions.correction: Electricity is a transfer route, not a store. While the current flows, work is done; the store that fills is the thermal store of the element and then of whatever it heats.

misconceptions.question: In ΔE = m c Δθ, which temperature goes into the equation?
misconceptions.correct: The temperature change Δθ, that is the final temperature minus the starting temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The final temperature reading, or sometimes the starting one, is substituted instead of the change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Δθ is written as a single symbol, and the question usually quotes two temperatures, so one of them is picked up unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: The Greek letter delta always means 'change in'. Subtract first, then substitute: water taken from 20 °C to 90 °C has Δθ = 70 °C, not 90 °C and not 20 °C.

misconceptions.question: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C. Can 4.2 be used instead?
misconceptions.correct: No, not with mass in kilograms and energy in joules. Using 4.2 makes the answer a thousand times too small.
misconceptions.misconception: The value 4.2 is substituted because it is the number the student has seen written down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 4.2 is the value in J/g °C, and it also appears as 4.2 kJ/kg °C, so the digits look familiar while the unit is skipped over.
misconceptions.correction: Always substitute the value with the unit that matches the other quantities. With mass in kg and the answer wanted in J, the specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C.

misconceptions.question: In W = F s, how are the force and the distance combined?
misconceptions.correct: They are multiplied. Work done equals force multiplied by distance moved along the line of the force.
misconceptions.misconception: The two numbers are combined by the wrong operation: divided one way, inverted the other way, or simply added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most equations met just before this one, such as speed and density, are divisions, so division becomes the default action on a pair of numbers, and a weak candidate who cannot recall the operation adds them instead.
misconceptions.correction: Read the equation as it is written: F s means F multiplied by s. A larger force over a longer distance must do more work, so dividing cannot be right.

misconceptions.question: A 2000 W kettle runs for 90 s. Is the energy transferred 2000 ÷ 90?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rearranging P = E / t gives E = P t, so the energy transferred is 2000 × 90.
misconceptions.misconception: Power and energy are treated as the same quantity, or the equation is rearranged the wrong way round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are quoted in questions about appliances, and P = E / t contains a division, so a division is carried out on whichever numbers are given.
misconceptions.correction: Power is energy transferred each second, so running for longer must transfer more energy. Multiply the power by the time in seconds.

misconceptions.question: On a common scale diagram, must the bars after a change add up to the bars before?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The total is the same before and after; only the way it is shared between stores has changed.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the useful output needs to be shown, so the bars after the change are allowed to add up to less.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams in advertising and in some textbooks show only the useful output, and the dissipated energy is left off because it is not wanted.
misconceptions.correction: Draw every bar, including the thermal store of the surroundings. The diagram is a way of showing that the total is redistributed, and it only works if nothing is left out.

misconceptions.question: If an object is present during a change, must one of its stores be changing?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the stores that actually empty or fill are named; everything else is left out.
misconceptions.misconception: A store is named for any object that happens to be involved, even when that store is not changing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn to label diagrams with stores and feel that every object in the picture needs one, so a store is attached to the nearest available object.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what would have to be true for that store to change: has the object moved faster, been raised, been stretched, or become warmer? If the answer is no, the store is not part of the description.

misconceptions.question: In P = E / t, what unit must the time be in?
misconceptions.correct: Seconds, so that the power in watts gives the energy in joules.
misconceptions.misconception: The time is substituted in minutes or hours without being converted to seconds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday times are quoted in minutes, and the equation itself contains no reminder that t must be in seconds.
misconceptions.correction: Convert first, then substitute. 90 s stays as 90; 1.5 minutes must become 90 s before it is used.

misconceptions.question: Is temperature the same thing as energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Temperature tells you how hot something is; the thermal store tells you how much energy it holds.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating an object raises its temperature without transferring any energy to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature is the quantity that is measured and talked about, so it takes the place of energy in students' descriptions of heating.
misconceptions.correction: Heating is an energy transfer, and a rise in temperature is the evidence that the thermal store has filled. Two objects at the same temperature can hold very different amounts of energy.

mcqs.stem: In physics, what is meant by a system?

options.text: An object, or a group of objects, being studied.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: a system is an object or group of objects.

options.text: A machine that has been built to move energy.
options.rationale: The everyday sense of 'system' as a manufactured device is carried into physics.

options.text: A group of two or more objects, never one.
options.rationale: The word 'group' is remembered but the alternative 'an object' is dropped.

options.text: A place where energy is kept until used.
options.rationale: System and store are treated as the same idea; a store is a way energy is held, not the thing being studied.

mcqs.stem: What always happens when a system changes?

options.text: Some of the energy in the system is used up.
options.rationale: 'Using up' energy is everyday language, but nothing is consumed.

options.text: The way energy is stored in the system changes.
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification says happens when a system changes.

options.text: The amount of energy in the system rises.
options.rationale: A change is assumed to add energy; the total is redistributed, not increased.

options.text: Extra energy is created inside the system itself.
options.rationale: Energy cannot be created; the stores simply hold it differently.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a way of storing energy rather than a way of transferring it?

options.text: The heating of a large beaker of cold water.
options.rationale: Heating is one of the transfer routes named in this section, not a store.

options.text: The work done by a steady pushing force.
options.rationale: Work done by a force is a transfer route; the store it fills is the kinetic store.

options.text: The elastic store of a squashed spring.
options.rationale: A stretched or squashed spring holds energy, so this is a store.

options.text: An electric current in a copper wire.
options.rationale: A current is the means by which work is done; there is no electrical store.

mcqs.stem: The specification asks for all the changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. What must such a description name?

options.text: Only the store that empties during the change.
options.rationale: Naming what empties is half a description; the destination is missing.

options.text: Only the useful store that fills in the change.
options.rationale: Only the wanted outcome is described, so dissipation to thermal stores is left out.

options.text: The size of the force that is acting on the system.
options.rationale: Force is offered in place of energy; a description of stores does not need it.

options.text: Each store that empties and each that fills.
options.rationale: 'All the changes' means both ends of every transfer are named.

mcqs.stem: A ball is thrown straight upwards. As it rises, what happens to the way energy is stored?

options.text: The gravitational store empties, the kinetic store fills.
options.rationale: The two stores are named correctly but the direction of the transfer is reversed.

options.text: The kinetic store empties and the gravitational store fills.
options.rationale: The ball slows as it gains height, so the kinetic store empties into the gravitational store.

options.text: The kinetic store keeps filling while the ball rises.
options.rationale: Movement is equated with a filling kinetic store, but the ball is slowing down.

options.text: Both the kinetic and the gravitational stores fill.
options.rationale: Energy would have to come from nowhere for both stores to fill.

mcqs.stem: Air resistance is ignored. At the highest point of a ball's flight, what has happened to the energy that was in its kinetic store?

options.text: It was destroyed at the moment the ball stopped.
options.rationale: Stopping is taken to mean the energy has gone, rather than moved.

options.text: It has been transferred to the elastic store of the air.
options.rationale: A store is named for the air even though nothing has been stretched or squashed.

options.text: Some remains, because the ball is still moving up.
options.rationale: At the highest point the ball is momentarily at rest, so the kinetic store is empty.

options.text: It has all been transferred to the gravitational store.
options.rationale: With no air resistance the whole of the kinetic store fills the gravitational store.

mcqs.stem: A trolley moving along a bench hits a wall and stops. What happens to the energy in its kinetic store?

options.text: It is transferred to thermal stores and by sound.
options.rationale: The trolley, the wall and the surrounding air warm slightly and a sound wave carries some energy away.

options.text: It is destroyed by the impact of the trolley on the wall.
options.rationale: The energy becomes hard to see, so it is assumed to have gone.

options.text: It is used up in bringing the trolley to a stop.
options.rationale: 'Used up' replaces a description of where the energy actually went.

options.text: It stays in the kinetic store of the stopped trolley.
options.rationale: A stationary trolley has an empty kinetic store.

mcqs.stem: A constant horizontal force pushes a box along a smooth, level floor. Which store fills as the box speeds up?

options.text: The gravitational store of the moving box.
options.rationale: The floor is level, so the height of the box does not change.

options.text: The chemical store of the pushing force.
options.rationale: A force is treated as something that holds energy.

options.text: The kinetic store of the moving box.
options.rationale: Work done by the force transfers energy to the kinetic store as the box speeds up.

options.text: The elastic store of the smooth floor.
options.rationale: The floor is in the picture, so a store is attached to it; nothing is stretched or squashed.

mcqs.stem: A car slows down when the driver brakes. Which statement describes the changes in the way energy is stored?

options.text: The kinetic store empties into the chemical store of the brakes.
options.rationale: The brakes are correctly identified, but friction does not fill a chemical store.

options.text: Energy is lost from the car, so the total energy falls.
options.rationale: 'Lost' is taken literally; the energy has been dissipated, not removed.

options.text: The kinetic store empties and the thermal stores of the brakes fill.
options.rationale: Friction at the brakes does work, filling thermal stores of the brakes, tyres, road and air.

options.text: The kinetic store of the car fills as it keeps moving.
options.rationale: Motion is misread as the kinetic store still filling, though it empties.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist stops pedalling on level ground and slowly freewheels to a stop. Which store empties?

options.text: The kinetic store of the cyclist and the bicycle.
options.rationale: Friction and air resistance do work, emptying the kinetic store into thermal stores.

options.text: The chemical store held in the cyclist's leg muscles.
options.rationale: The cyclist is present, so a store is named for them; pedalling has stopped, so this store is not emptying.

options.text: The gravitational store of the moving bicycle.
options.rationale: The ground is level, so the height of the bicycle does not change.

options.text: No store keeps it, the energy is lost to the surroundings.
options.rationale: Treats dissipated energy as simply lost rather than stored in surroundings.

mcqs.stem: Water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle. Which statement describes the main change in the way energy is stored?

options.text: The chemical store of the kettle itself empties into the water.
options.rationale: The chemical store is the familiar source, but the kettle holds no fuel.

options.text: The water gains a store of electrical energy as it is heated.
options.rationale: 'Electrical energy' is treated as a store rather than a transfer route.

options.text: The kinetic store of the water fills as the water boils.
options.rationale: Bubbling looks like movement, but the store that fills is the thermal store.

options.text: The current does work and the water's thermal store fills.
options.rationale: A current in the element does work; the thermal stores of the element and then the water fill.

mcqs.stem: As well as the water, which other thermal stores fill while a kettle boils?

options.text: Only the water's store; nothing else becomes warm.
options.rationale: Only the wanted outcome is counted, so the rest of the redistribution is ignored.

options.text: Those of the kettle and of the air around it.
options.rationale: The element, the kettle body and the surrounding air all end up warmer.

options.text: None, because the water uses up all the energy.
options.rationale: 'Used up' again replaces an account of where the energy went.

options.text: Those of the mains cable and the power supply.
options.rationale: Stores are named for objects outside the change being described; the supply does not warm because this water boils.

mcqs.stem: 0.50 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Using ΔE = m c Δθ, what is the change in thermal energy?

options.rationale: The specific heat capacity has been taken as 4.2 instead of 4200 J/kg °C.
Only m and c have been multiplied; the temperature change has been left out.
The starting temperature of 20 °C has been used in place of the 70 °C change.

mcqs.stem: A heater is switched on under a beaker of water. What does heating the water do?

options.text: It raises its temperature but transfers no energy.
options.rationale: Temperature is treated as a separate thing from energy.

options.text: It fills the kinetic store of the beaker.
options.rationale: The beaker is present, so a store is named for it; the beaker as a whole does not move.

options.text: It transfers energy to the water's thermal store.
options.rationale: Heating is a transfer route, and the store it fills is the thermal store of the water.

options.text: It uses up energy inside the water each second.
options.rationale: Nothing is consumed; the thermal store of the water fills.

mcqs.stem: A constant force of 40 N pushes a crate 2.5 m across a floor, in the direction of the force. Using W = F s, how much work is done?

options.rationale: The force has been divided by the distance instead of multiplied by it.
The two given values have been added rather than multiplied.
The equation has been inverted, giving distance divided by force.

mcqs.stem: A constant resultant force does work on an object moving horizontally along the line of the force. What does this work do?

options.text: It fills the kinetic store of the object.
options.rationale: Work done by a resultant force along the motion transfers energy to the kinetic store.

options.text: It is stored as force inside the moving object.
options.rationale: Force is treated as a quantity an object can hold.

options.text: It uses up the energy the object already has.
options.rationale: Work done here adds to a store rather than consuming energy.

options.text: It makes the object rise as its kinetic store fills.
options.rationale: Conflates kinetic gain with upward motion, so work is imagined to lift it.

mcqs.stem: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 90 s. Using P = E / t, how much energy is transferred by the current?

options.rationale: P = E / t rearranges to E = P t, so E = 2000 × 90 = 180 000 J.
The power has been divided by the time instead of multiplied by it.
The time has been read as 1.5 minutes and used without converting it to seconds.
The equation has been inverted, giving time divided by power.

mcqs.stem: A current flows through the heating element of a hairdryer. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The element holds a store of electrical energy inside itself.
options.rationale: 'Electrical energy' is treated as something the element keeps.

options.text: The current is used up as it passes through the element.
options.rationale: Current is confused with energy, and neither is consumed.

options.text: The current does work, filling the element's thermal store.
options.rationale: Work done when a current flows is the transfer route; the thermal store fills.

options.text: The chemical store of the metal wire empties into it.
options.rationale: The chemical store is offered as a source, but nothing reacts in the wire.

mcqs.stem: An energy diagram drawn to a common scale shows the stores in a system before and after a change. What must be true of the bars?

options.text: The total after the change must be smaller than before.
options.rationale: Dissipated energy is assumed to have left the diagram altogether.

options.text: Every bar after the change matches a bar before it.
options.rationale: The individual bars change size; it is only the total that is preserved.

options.text: The useful output bar must equal the input bar.
options.rationale: Only the wanted output is drawn, so the dissipated share is missing.

options.text: The bars after the change add to the same total.
options.rationale: A common scale shows the same total redistributed between different stores.

mcqs.stem: A lamp is supplied with 500 J of energy. It transfers 60 J to the surroundings by light. Drawn on a common scale, what must the remaining bar show?

options.text: 560 J, the two amounts added together.
options.rationale: The input and the output have been added instead of compared.

options.text: 440 J, going to thermal stores.
options.rationale: 500 − 60 = 440 J, which fills thermal stores of the lamp and the surroundings.

options.text: 60 J, the same as the light output.
options.rationale: The two bars are assumed to be equal without checking the total.

options.text: Nothing, the energy has been used up.
options.rationale: The missing 440 J is assumed to have gone rather than been dissipated.
